sections.heading: Support For Children In Hardship Bill

items.text: First Reading

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That the Support
for Children in Hardship Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Social Services
Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time, I intend to move that the bill be
reported by 3 November 2015.
The Support for Children in Hardship Bill and the Budget package it supports represent
the next step in this Government’s strong and continuing programme to tackle material
hardship for children in low-income families. Introducing this omnibus bill under urgency
will allow the greatest possible time in select committee while ensuring the bill can be
passed into law by the end of the year to be implemented from 1 April 2016. The bill
amends the Social Security Act, inland revenue Acts, and the Education Act,  delivering
key components of this Government’s $790 million Budget package. The provisions in
the bill build on the firm foundations this Government has laid down by creating a strong
economy that supports more jobs and higher incomes for working families , by setting
clear targets for public services to address root causes of material hardship for children,
and by continuing our welfare reform’s unrelenting focus on work, ensuring those who
are able do all they can to find work, helping themselves and their children get ahead.
Welfare reform is working. In 2010 we introduced part -time work obligations for
parents on a benefit with a youngest child aged 6 or over. As sound management saw the
economy strengthen and job opportunities grow, we extended this obligation to include
beneficiaries with a child over 5 years of age. The results are clear. Since 2010 there has
been a 19 percent drop in the number of people on sole parent support benefit. That means
there are 16,500 fewer people on sole parent support, resulting in the lowest  sole parent
benefit numbers since the 1980s. This bill seeks to extend and accelerate those gains. It
mirrors the growing and strengthening economy and labour market by expanding work
obligations for beneficiary parents. From 1 April 2016 they will be req uired to start
looking for part-time work when their youngest child is 3 and 4 years of age. This is a
time in which both parents in the majority of two -parent families are in part or full -time
work. Our expectation and aspiration for those on benefits should be the same. This will
see another 18,000 beneficiary parents brought into the part-time work obligations group.
This is where case management focused on work is the strongest and where additional
resources have been provided through the Budget package.
We also know that there are important benefits for children attending high -quality
early childhood education by 3 years of age, which is why this Government provides for
20 hours of early childhood education. Research shows us that children in more
vulnerable families, including beneficiary households, have the most to gain. Alongside
this change, the bill amends the definition of part -time work within the Social Security
Act. Currently, part -time work is defined in the benefits system as being work that
averages 15 hours per week. From 1 April 2016, this bill increases that to 20 hours per
week. At 20 hours’ part -time work, most beneficiary parents will be better off, and off
benefits, thanks to a combination of earned income and increased tax credits. Incr easing
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3567
the part -time work obligation to 20 hours a week means a greater attachment to the
workforce. In addition, most sole parents working 20 hours or more a week will be better
off with a mixture of wages and Working for Families tax credits than they are on benefits.
This is a strong incentive to leave the benefit altogether.
Flexibility will be maintained regarding the exact hours of work, to take account of
individual factors and particular job opportunities. We know, however, that the costs of
childcare can lessen the rewards of employment for many low -income working parents,
including beneficiaries moving into work. With this in mind, the Budget package
introduces a new, higher rate of assistance for up to 50 hours a week of childcare or out-
of-school care focused on helping the lowest-income working families. The significance
of this change should not be underestimated. It is delivering an average gain of over $23
a week for each family. The childcare increase in the Budget package will be delivered
by amendments to regulations rather than requiring amendments through this bill.
Turning now to benefit rates, on 1 April 2016 core benefit rates for each beneficiary
household with dependent children will increase by $25 per week on top of the CPI
increase that year. This is the first lift in core benefit rates since 1972 for benefici aries
with dependent children. This will deliver some of the rewards of a strong economy
directly to New Zealand’s lowest -income households and the 194,000 children within
them. The bill amends the schedules of the Social Security Act that set out benefit rates,
enacting the increase to core benefit rates for families with children on 1 April 2016 and,
where necessary, creating specific rates for households with one or more children where
none exist now. A similar increase will be made to allowances for students with dependent
children, both to ensure that the children of low-income students share these gains and to
reward students’ efforts through study, rather than creating an incentive to move back on
to a benefit. This increase to student allowances will  also occur through regulations and
will also be in addition to the consumer price increase.
The core of the package and the bill is balancing more assistance and expectations for
families with children while out of work, with increased financial support to enter and
stay in employment. We know that working families with children can struggle, often as
they enter work, and their combined incomes are low. That is why, with our childcare and
tax credit changes, over $300 million within the package is focused on ensuring that work
pays for low-income families with children and that their incomes lift,  helping to ensure
they can meet the needs of their children in a way we all expect to.
Tax credit increases from 1 April 2016 for working families with children will provide
$12.50 a week more in the base rate of the in-work tax credit, delivering that full gain to
families earning $36,350 or less a year. It will also provide families earnin g more than
$36,350 a year with an increase in their in -work tax credit, which could be less than
$12.50 depending on their exact income, and provide an extra $12 a week to working
families who earn less than $27,000 a year and are receiving the minimum fa mily tax
credit so that, combined with the in -work tax credit, these families’ weekly incomes are
increased by $24.50. Together, these changes will benefit over 203,000 low -income
working families and their 383,000 children.
To ensure that taxpayers’ investment is well targeted to lower-income families, the bill
at the same time increases the abatement rate for Working for Families payments by 1.25
percentage points and advances the timing of future changes to abatement rates and
thresholds. A final provision in the bill, as with every other major benefit and tax credit
change, provides a backstop that can cover exceptional circumstances and any unintended
consequences due to the complexity of the tax and benefit system. Taken together, this
bill and the Budget package it supports will mean that almost every low -income New
Zealand family with children will be better off.
I commend the Support for Children in Hardship Bill to the House.
3568 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: There are many reasons why various members of
Parliament come into this place or enter into politics. Child poverty has always been one
of my main motivations, and it is helpful, perhaps, in that regard, that child poverty is one
of those issues that are man-made. If we are looking for an issue where the Government
absolutely can make a difference, it is an issue like child poverty. But how to make that
difference is the question that those who are interested in this area grapple with. Well,
helpfully, the  evidence—the numbers; the whole picture that is built out of those
statistics—tells us exactly what we as politicians need to do. That is what makes this area
so frustrating. There are 260,000 children in need, and we know exactly what we need to
do to help them. I would liken it also, perhaps, to knowing where there might be a site of
frequent car crashes—where there are continual accidents because there is a blind spot.
You go begging to the Government to fix the blind spot. Well, today the Government has
put up a sign.
Let us be clear that any extra support that is going into the homes of vulnerable families
is absolutely welcomed. This side of the House welcomes the fact that the Government
has today—in my mind, really, for the first time —genuinely acknowledged that there is
severe hardship and poverty in New Zealand. But now that it has acknowledged there is
a problem, it has an absolute obligation and responsibility to do more, because that is
what the evidence tells us we need to do.
The first thing we know from the numbers —the measures of persistent poverty —is
that the longest period of time when hardship is experienced in a child’s life is actually
when that child is first born. That, we also know, is the most critical time of a child’s life.
Instinct will probably tell you that that hardship is most often going to be the situation of
sole parents. It is harder for them to go to work because they are the sole caregiver, and
that poverty generally lasts for 3 to 4 years, in those earliest years of that child’s life. So,
yes, giving those families an extra $25 a week is a good thing, but let us also be realistic.
For a family with one child, $25 is great. What about families with two children or three
children? That payment is per family, not per child. This is the point the Children’s
Commissioner was right to make. It is, ultimately, roughly enough for a large pack of
nappies for a week.
In the Labour Party, we looked at the evidence too. That is why, when we developed
the Best Start package, we thought that we needed to give those families $60 a week, that
we needed to give that per child, and that we needed to make sure it lasted for at least the
first 3 years of that child’s life. That was what Best Start absolutely did. It was targeted,
but it was more generous. That is what the evidence absolutely told us to do. In the Labour
Party, we also recognised that that is one part of the picture. The second part of the picture
is that there are families in poverty who are working. This Government has said
persistently that the way to get out of poverty is to get into work. If only that were true,
but that is not what our economy is delivering for New Zealand families. Two out of five
families living in poverty are in work.
Not all work is born equal in New Zealand. Not all work is decent work. Not all work
means that families are free from the burden of poverty, and that is why we absolutely
needed a Government today that acknowledged that —that looked at the evidence from
the Growing Up in New Zealand report, which said that some families are working
multiple jobs just to survive. In part, this bill potentially exacerbates that problem. Yes,
the Government is giving a bit of extra support in welfare for families, but it is also placing
extra work obligations on parents of children—no longer at the age of 5, but at the age of
3. That does not acknowledge the reality for many of our sole parent caregivers. Finding
a job is one thing, but we must point out that in this Budget there is nothing about creating
work.
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3569
Last year 41 percent of jobs in New Zealand were created by whom? Small businesses.
They get nothing in this Budget. If you want to help families to find work, then help the
people who create the jobs that they move into. Finding jobs is one thing, but making sure
that those jobs are paying decently is another. Also, making sure that the hours that you
find in those part -time jobs fit in with your early childhood education care is another
question entirely. Part-time work is often at hours that are not family and child - friendly.
Again, we need to be realistic about the kind of environment that these parents are going
to be operating in. Labour has serious reservations about this element of the bill, and this
is exactly what we will be looking at in the select committee.
It is also about the bigger picture. The evidence has always said that to tackle child
poverty, you need a plan. In the wake of this Budget, the Children’s Commissioner has
today said that this extra payment, although good, does not constitute a plan. A ge nuine
plan that really wants to fix child poverty would make housing affordable. We know it is
a fact that some families are using 50 percent of their income just to make sure that they
have a roof over their heads, and sometimes that roof is damp and it i s cold and it is
crowded. If we are genuinely addressing child poverty, we need to make sure that housing
is affordable and available to those families. That should have been part of the plan.
We need to make sure that health care is genuinely accessible. Some of these families
are experiencing such dire circumstances that even though it might be free for their child
to go to the doctor, the parent who is meant to take them has debt at their local clinic and
so does not go because they know that they will not be able to get an appointment before
paying their debt. I have heard of stories of families who have lost their jobs and whose
kids have contracted scabies. Although they have managed to go and get the treatment
for them, they cannot even afford the hot water that is required to do the hot -water wash
to rid the family of that affliction. Poverty is a vicious cycle, and it never affects just one
part of a family’s life.
We would also be making sure, if we had a genuine plan, that we address the hidden
costs of education and make it accessible. Labour was committed, and remains
committed, to a full whole -of-Government plan. We have a bill in the ballot called the
Child Pov erty Reduction and Eradication Bill. It is all about making sure that the
Ministers for housing, education, health, social development, and finance all have
responsibility for a package that deals with child poverty. For us, Best Start —that $566
million pa ckage—was only one part of the picture, and for this Government, this bill
should be only one part of the picture.

items.speaker: One extra thing
items.text: on child poverty, a critical difference between us and this Government
is that we are willing to put  in place the target. We are willing to put a number to how
much we are committed to reducing child poverty by. Why has that Government not done
it? I know, from having done numbers for ourselves, how hard it is to genuinely lift a
family out of poverty, and this measure today will not do it. It just will not, and we will
report on how much we do on that target in every single Budget.
I leave my final words for the place where this all started for me. I talk a lot about
having spent a few years as a child living in a town called Murupara. The people in
Murupara who found themselves in hardship found themselves in that place, ultimately,
because their region and their town were dependent on forestry. In the 1980s that industry
was absolutely gutted for them. That was what ultimately drove the poverty in that town.
A measure like this today will not solve that problem for the people of a t own like
Murupara. We need, ultimately, an economy that works for everyone and that gives
people hope. Today the Government acknowledged that we have a problem, but, sadly, it
did not fix it.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise to take a call on the Support for Children in
Hardship Bill in its first reading. As the chair, I look forward to the bill coming to the
3570 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
Social Services Committee, a very hard -working committee that looks forward to the
debate, to the deliberation, and also to hearing the submissions. It is always good to speak
after the member Miss Ardern. She commented about the blind spot in regard to poverty
and the intention coming to this House. I remember in the 2014 elections at one of the
debates around poverty, she was challenged about the fact that 142,000 children were still
in poverty during the time of the Labour Government. Her response was th is: “It was a
job unfinished.” —it was a job unfinished. So although the talk is about children in
poverty, there was a job that was unfinished by the Labour Government, which talked
about that. When talking about figures, it is interesting that those membe rs are talking
about that now.
The issue about a plan —this is a plan. As the Minister of Finance said, this is a plan
that is working for our children in hardship and for our families as well. How do we
know? Well, we can talk about ours—and I will in a moment—but in its state of the nation
speech, A Mountain All Can Climb, out of the 22 indicators, the Salvation Army gave us
the thumbs up on 14 of them. I just recall, at a glance, that with regard to child poverty,
it was thumbs up for reducing it by 2 percent. With regard to children at risk, there was a
reduction of 15 percent. I could go on. There were 15 indicators by the Salvation Army
with regard to the reduction of child poverty.
As this bill comes to the House, I say it is a good bill. Can I commend the Minister for
Social Development, the honourable Minister Tolley, for the work that she has done to
put this together. Can I also acknowledge our previous Minister for Social Development,
the honourable Minister Paula Bennett, who is here as well, for the work that she has done
and for the leadership that she has taken for us as well. It was great to hear from the Hon
Te Ururoa Flavell, and this is what he said. He said that it has taken almost 43 years—in
fact, back to 1972—since the base benefit rate was actually increased. Under a National
Government, that is what has happened. What is it doing? It is doing this. As the Minister
has said, there is a vision and a plan for reducing h ardship for children, and that is what
this bill is intending to do. It has a theme that I think is really important. It is this: your
circumstances should not define your destiny. I think that is very important.
Part of the amendments in this bill, which is an omnibus bill, are around the Social
Security Act of 1964. If I quote from the Act, in Part 1, which is its purpose and intent,
there is section 1A(a)(ii). It indicates that the purpose of the Social Security  Act of 1964
is “to help people to find or retain paid employment;”. Section 1A(ca) says it is “to
provide services to encourage and help young persons to move to education, training, and
employment …”. I mention these because I think it is important for t he public to know
that the bill at hand is in line with the intentions, the purpose, and the principles of the
Social Security Act, which are to provide opportunities for employment for those who are
actually in need, as well. We know that employment lifts  our families out of hardship.
We think that is important. The bill is a balanced mix of greater work expectations. Two-
thirds of children are living in hardship and we think that that is important —80,000 are
in sole parent families, hence the reason why t his bill is focused on that. We know that
nine to 10 of those children are from sole parent families, and we think that that is
important as well.
So we think that this bill will go to the select committee. We look forward to the
submissions. The benefit rates, we think, are going to be quite important news to our
communities. Can I finally just conclude my remarks briefly, because I think this bill is
due for its reading and its referral to the select committee, by saying that the comments
that are made about children in poverty are often made about Māori and Pacific children.
It concerns me that in our communities, a stigma is created by the Opposit ion about that
when there is all the talk, there is all the rhetoric, but there is not the plan to be able to
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3571
make a difference. I believe that this bill and its intentions will absolutely make a
difference to those families that we are talking about.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Now, you’re just not telling the truth, Alfred.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I look forward to this bill. I look forward to the debate, even if
Ms Ardern returns to the Social Services Committee as well. I think that this is going to
be good news for our communities. I look forward to the discussions and the submissions,
and I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: I just want to start by talking to some
of the points made by the former speaker, Alfred Ngaro. No one at all —at all—on this
side of the House today has referred to, or stigmatised, Māori and Pacific with regard to
poverty. It was he who decided to bring that up. In fact, we are talking about children in
poverty more widely. It does not matter what ethnicity they are. We are talking about
children in poverty and the obligation and the responsibility that we have here, not just
the Government but the entire Parliament, to make sure that we are responding to the
needs of children in poverty. Even just looking at the title of this bill, the Support for
Children in Hardship Bill, I cannot help but say we all need to remember that these
children come from households with caregivers who are also experiencing hardship.
When we talk about supporting these children, we do need to be talking about how we
can support the people who are looking after them to take them out of hardship. We, of
course, support any measure that will put money into the pockets of New Zealanders
experiencing hardship—New Zealanders who are our most vulnerable. However, this bill
does come with conditions that could have repercussions and those are the repercussions
that I want to talk about today. Those are the things we need to think about and consider
as we look to push this bill through.
Labour is concerned about the implementation of the proposed work obligations on
parents. It is not that we do not support parents going out into the workforce. It is not that
we do not think that it is a good thing for parents to be out in the workforce. It is just that
when you are saying to parents that no longer is it that when their children are 5 years old
they have to go and look for part -time work, it is at 3 years old, then there are
repercussions. We have heard widely in the media lately that ther e are real issues with
things like accessibility to quality childcare arrangements, accessibility to quality early
childhood education. Unfortunately, many of the areas where we have people living in
hardship are the areas where those people have less acce ss to quality early childhood
education. When you put these parents in the position of having to, being forced to, go
out to work when their child is only 3, then you are also forcing them, possibly, to put
their children into substandard childcare arrange ments, into centres that they are not
comfortable with, into centres that they are not sure about the quality of, and that is
something that we should be concerned about. No parent should be forced to put their
child into an early childcare centre if they are not sure about the quality that will be
provided there to that child.
The support that will be required for these particular parents, particularly sole parents,
to actually get into the part-time work that will suit their circumstances is quite immense.
These parents need part -time work that fits within particular hours beca use of the
childcare arrangements that they have. They may have an older child who goes to school
from 9 to 3. They may want to fit it into that time frame—it makes sense. They may need
flexibility, more flexibility in their work, because of the fact that we know that the
younger the child —any parent knows this —the more likely they are to get sick,
particularly when they are going to early childcare centres. Things just tend to float
around. So they are going to need work that will give them that flexibility. They are going
to need work that will, hopefully, be secure and give them the money that will ensure that
they are actually going out of hardship. But what really concerns me is that here we have
3572 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
this move to push sole parents out into work, increasing the obligations around work, but
at the same time what we see in this Budget is an actual $91 million cut to the job seeker
budget. So here we have higher expectations on these parents, but then a cut to the support
that they will be getting from the State to actually get into the work that they are required
to take up.
I can only presume that the $91 million cut to jobseeker support, which is in this
Budget, is because that Government thinks that the total number of beneficiaries is going
down. But we have seen research around the future of work, around the increasing issues
we are going to have for security in work, around the changes in the nature of jobs that
are out there, and the fact is that, actually, we may see more and more people going in
and out of employment because of the changing nature of work. So to cut $9 1 million
from the job seeker budget when the Government is extending the obligations on sole
parents around working, as well as the fact that we know that moving forward there are
real issues with regard to the future of work and the security of work, is actually a little
bit negligent, I think, of that Government. To say that work is important, to continually
rattle off the importance of work for beneficiaries, but to cut $91 million from the job
seeker budget is a little bit irresponsible of that Government.
We support the idea that an additional $25 will be going into the pockets of
beneficiaries every week. It is not a lot of money to many people here in this House, but
to beneficiaries it will make a little bit of a difference. But we do need to refer back to the
policy that we had, leading into the last election, where we actually had committed to
putting in an additional $60 into the pockets of beneficiaries with children under the age
of 3. That would have made much more of a difference. As my colleague J acinda has
said—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: —the $25 extra that these beneficiaries will be receiving will
actually not even come close to taking them out of poverty. When Government members
talk about addressing the hardship, when they talk about addressing the poverty, we
actually need to see, as the Children’s Commissioner has said, a real plan, not just a few
sticky plasters. This is really what it is. It is not even a packet of sticky plasters. It is one
sticky plaster that is going to come off the scab and then there is nothing to replace it and
nothing is actually better.
We acknowledge, and are very glad with, the Government’s announcement that
National has finally acknowledged that Working for Families lifts incomes, and it has
continued with Labour’s sensible economic policy. What did they call it at the time?
When we in troduced Working for Families, when we were in Government, National
referred to it as—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Communism by stealth.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Communism by stealth.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: John Key.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: John Key himself referred to Working for Families as
communism by stealth. So it is heartening to know that eventually National has come
round to the fact that it is Labour’s policies that are responsible, that are effective, and
that actually are all about good economic management of this country.
I just want to refer back to the fact that we are talking about parents being obligated to
go out to work. So they will be required to put their children into early childhood
education from the age of 3 so that they can take up that part -time work. I just want to
say that when it comes to early childhood education, when it comes to the arrangements
around supporting sole parents, it was Labour before the last election that proposed
extending the subsidy for early childhood education to 25 hours a week. It w as Labour
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3573
that wanted to extend the provisions around parental leave. It was Labour that wanted to
introduce a $60 a week Best Start payment for children under the age of 3.
So I do want to acknowledge that, yes, it is a surprise, as the Children’s Commissioner
has said, that National has done this, that it has decided that $25 extra a week for a
beneficiary is a good thing, but, as the Children’s Commissioner said, this is a surprise
but it is not a plan. As my colleague Jacinda has said—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: —Jacinda Ardern has said—this will not effectively address
the issue that we face of child poverty. It will not necessarily address the issues that the
260,000 children who are living in poverty in New Zealand are faced with every day.
We will be supporting this bill. We have reservations about this bill, particularly with
regard to the obligations on sole parents to go out to work —not work in general but just
the extension of the work obligations—but because of the fact that it does put  a little bit
more money into the pockets of beneficiaries, we will be supporting this bill.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: It gives me great honour to rise and
support the first reading of the Support for Children in Hardship Bill. As a first -term
member of Parliament and hearing my first Budget, it was one of those moments where
time just seemed to stop. There was plenty of time to soak in all the news and all the
information. I think today will be a definitive point over the next year, over the next 2
years, and over the next 3 years. What I mean by that is that this Budget has proved that
the National Party is the working people’s party. We are out there working for the people
of New Zealand, but we are listening to the people of New Zealand. Why I know that we
are the working people’s party is that we have created over 194,000 jobs since 2011, and
we will go on to create tens of thousands more. That is important for this bill because we
know that job creation reduces child poverty.
The Budget announced a $790 million child hardship package. Working families who
earn less than $27,000 will get a $24.50 increase to their Working for Families payment
every week. That is 4,000 families. This National Government is the working people’s
party. Families earning $27,000 to $36,350 will get a $12.50 increase to their Working
for Families payment. That is 50,000 families in New Zealand.
When I campaigned last year I met many people who were voting National for the first
time. They had voted for Labour all their life but they knew that we were working for
New Zealanders and we were listening to New Zealanders. We are delivering better jobs
and better incomes. They said to us to support the most vulnerable. That is why for
beneficiary families—how much time?

items.speaker: Todd Muller
items.text: Keep going.

items.speaker: MATT DOOCEY
items.text: We are increasing the benefit by $25 every week. That is 110,000
families. I know that when we look back, we will know that we have worked hard for the
working people of New Zealand and we have listened to them.
I am proud of this National Government, which is working hard for the working people
of New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I would like to start my speech on this bill by paying tribute to
sole-parent families on a benefit who are struggling to do the best for their children, who
are parenting alone 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and who are struggling to be able to
put food on the table and feed their children. I acknowledge their children, all too many
of whom do not have a bed of their, who do not have enough to eat, who are surviving on
sandwiches because some days that is all that is left in the budget at the end of the week,
who do not get Christmas presents or birthday presents because there is not enough money
in the family budget to be able to pay for them, and who cannot afford schools trips. I
really want to acknowledge those children. I want to acknowledge the New Zealanders
who have been fighting for years and who have been raising their hearts to the
3574 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
Government to stand up to change this situation. The well -being of our children is the
soul of our country. When our children are suffering, we are suffering as a country. So I
want to acknowledge that fight and all those people who have forced the Government into
this measure, which is the first time that benefit rates have been increased since 1972.
The Greens have been raising issues of child poverty for over a decade now. We are
passionate about changing this reality because we know it is possible. Although we are
hearing from the Government that this is the first time since 1972 that benefit rates have
been increased, the Government is admitting the fact that it cut the benefits in 1990 and
that we are still not even returning, with this increase, to the level they were at in 1990.
For most families, this $25 is not actually $25, because this $25 will be eroded by cuts to
the accommodation supplement and the temporary additional assistance supplement,
which many families are using just to get by. So the $25 —which is the cost of, say,
nappies for one child —is not even going to be that much extra in th e hand for all too
many of our families. So when you think of those children who are going without shoes,
who are going out without raincoats, who are going without school trips, and who are
going without birthday presents and enough food to eat, we know t hat this is not the
answer. The Greens will support this bill because it is something. Those children need
something, but they deserve a whole lot more than this.
I also really just want to raise a very real concern that we have with this bill. It is
another example of the Government giving with one hand and taking with the other. What
this bill will do is require parents with children who are just 3 years old to go out and look
for 20 hours a week of work. Sole parents, who are doing the job of caring for their family
alone, are now going to be expected to be working for a minimum of 20 hours a week as
well as providing for the needs of their children. We know that that may actually mean a
reduction in their incomes because of the abatement on the benefits. It will work out to, I
think, about $2.20 an hour extra, if they are getting $15 an hour in those jobs. We know
most of those jobs, sadly, are at very minimum wag es. That is, actually, probably not
going to cover the cost of travel, childcare, or the clothes that are expected to be worn in
that job—let alone the extra needs of those children, to compensate for not having their
parent there. I really want to say tha t although we are hearing a lot in the House about
how we expect you to work if you can work, the Green Party believes that caring for
young children and children with complex needs is work. It is something that we value
and that we believe will pay off in the long term for the entire society if we support it.
As a society, we have no concept yet of what the consequences are going to be in 20
years’ time of a generation of adults, as they will be by that stage, who have not had time
with their parents, who have been in the care of strangers for so many hours a week, and
whose parents have lost out on the opportunity to participate in Playcentre, kōhanga reo,
or other family -centred childcare movements that have provided so much to our
communities and so much in terms of growing knowledge around parenting for thos e
families and our children. We have no concept yet of what the consequence will be of
separating parents from their children, as these kinds of policies are doing. I think it really,
really requires from this House and from the public some deep thought about this issue.
The Green Party will certainly not be supporting this bill past the select committee
stage unless this changes, because our children deserve at least one parent who is able to
be there for them in those early years. They deserve that ability for attachment  and
security. Again, as is my wont, I will remind this House that the indications are that of
sole parents, 70 percent are probably leaving violent relationships. Think of the needs of
those children and that woman—typically—to resettle themselves, to recover, to actually
bed in and get well and move on in their lives, and think about whether that is actually
possible while they are juggling the care of their children and working 20 hours a week.
I would say, from my experience of working with women in that situation, that for many
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3575
of them it is not possible, and the needs of their children will suffer. That will put many
women in a situation of feeling as if they are conflicted enough to go back into a
relationship that is not safe.
This bill raises many, many concerns for us, as a party and as a House. Also, I really
want to mention that while we are being told the Budget will also offer increases to
Working for Families, it is a little bit more complicated than that, in that the cha nge to
the abatement rate without changing the abatement threshold will result in a family with
one partner working being worse off than they currently are if their annual income
exceeds $36,406, or if they are getting $17.50 an hour. An extra 2c -per-hour income for
those people will eat up the entire $12.50 increase in the base rate for the in -work tax
credit component of Working for Families. With incomes still well below a living wage,
those people will actually be worse off under this proposed Working for Families regime.
So we are being told by this Government that it has suddenly got the message, that
everyone’s lobbying around the welfare of our children has got through —that the
Government has got it! It is making this change to Working for Families, but, in actual
fact, it is such a marginal change, and within that change some families are actually going
to be worse off.
I am pleased that this bill is not passing through all stages under urgency, because there
certainly seems to be enough in here that we need to look at really closely. To conclude,
I really want to go back to the fact that we have over a quarter of a million children living
in poverty in this country —between 60,000 and 100,000 without decent shoes, without
enough to eat, without Christmas or birthday presents, or without warm clothes or a bed
of their own. Those children need us to fix this problem, and, sa dly, this bill will not fix
this problem.

items.speaker: DARROCH BALL
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand First
to address this bill. We will be opposing the bill for a couple of very good reasons. Before
I get into the reasons why, I would like to go back to the actual speech that the Minister
of Finance gave today.

items.speaker: Delivering Better Public Services
items.text: put aside, for a second, the actual Public Service
targets that this Government has, which it established in 2008, which have never been
independently reviewed, and which I have asked both Minister Tolley and the Minister
of Finance about having reviewed and have been refused. Put that aside. There is a
quotation here from a speech given earlier today, which I would like to share. I think it
gives a definite perspective to the priority that this Government has. It goes lik e this:
“We’re willing to pay a bit more upfront to get real, sustainable change, and in doing so
we can generate significant long -term savings for the Crown.”  In the same sentence, in
the same breath, we have Mr English purporting that the intent of his bill is to have some
real, sustainable change for the future, but in the same breath he is mentioning the long -
term savings for the Crown. And that set up the t heme of his speech today, under
delivering Better Public Services for this country. Because in ev ery single sentence he
said, in every single paragraph, the Budget was about cost-cutting, it was about saving, it
was about dressing up the real needs and the real changes that need to happen to solve
child poverty —one of the major priorities that he said  the Government was going to
have—into cost-cutting measures and long-term savings for the Crown.
I would also like to give a little bit of perspective to this bill and to the speech that Mr
English gave today by using a little bit of a measuring stick. In regard to the child hardship
package, which recognises lower -income working parents, the total pa ckage is around
$240 million in each full year. The measuring stick that I would like to use is the flag
referendum, which will cost just under $30 million. That is more than 10 percent of the
total that this package is going to cost each year. Where is the priority of this Government?
He goes on to say that the Budget also provides a new operating fund of $36 million. We
3576 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
have got a flag referendum of just under $30 million: where is the priority of this
Government in dealing seriously with child hardship? We have new funding for the
existing Children’s Team that he was talking about. It gives an extra $23 million. That is
even less than what is going towards the flag referendum. So where is the priority that Mr
English purported he had for solving child poverty, for giving more to the needy in our
country? New Zealand First says that it evaporated as soon as he opened his mouth.
The questions that came out of both the bill and the speech that was delivered today
were, first of all: why have these changes occurred? Was it because there was a need for
them to occur? Was it because the Government can now afford for them to occur? Or was
it because the Government really has no choice but to make those changes now? What
rolls out of that is: why has it taken 7 years in Government for these changes to occur?
Increasing the minimum benefit levels is a step in the right direction, as we ha ve heard
from a couple of my colleagues in the House already. But the step that has been taken —
is it enough? Of course, it is not. New Zealand First believes that there should be a
minimum social floor that no one should fall below. It should not be a rewa rd. It should
not be a punishment. That is what is happening at the moment. That is what this
Government delivered in the Budget speech today. The benefit should be a safety net. It
should be strong, it should have integrity, and it should have the ability to not allow people
to slip through and live in poverty. That is what is happening right now, and that is what
will happen even after these Budget changes occur. The Government has the absolute
responsibility to not allow supported poverty to occur. That is what has been happening,
and that is why it will continue to happen with this Budget.
The Minister also talked about investment in the front end, and I would like to quote:
“We’re willing to pay” —like I said before —“a bit more upfront to get real, sustainable
change”. But what this is is plugging the gap. We have heard about a plaster over a wound,
but this is plugging a gap with the minimum amount of financial assistance. This is
addressing the symptoms; it is not addressing the causes. New Zealand First believes that
the major priority should be investing in the front end, before individuals need to end up
being caught by that safety net. The priorities should be investing in our youth and our
young people, especially unemployed youth and young people. That is the front -end
investment. The KiwiSaver kick-start contribution is an example of front-end investment,
and that is now gone. Job creation for our young people is front-end investment, and that
is now gone. What we have here is a carrot-and-stick approach from this Government. It
is quite simple: the number of unemployed youth  is at one of the highest levels that we
have had. It is steady and has not changed over the last 7 years that the National Party has
been in Government. Unemployed youth will become unemployed adults. And as the
Minister himself said today, two-thirds of all children in material hardship are living with
a parent on a benefit. That is the end result. That is the symptom. So why is this
Government concentrating on the end symptom and not the cause, and not on investing
in the real front end of this issue?
I would also just like to mention Working for Families and families earning $36,000 a
year. Low-income working families earning $36,000 a year, before tax, will get $12.50 a
week extra, but what does that mean in real terms? It is just over a 1 percent increase. If
we compare that, for example, with the cost of fruit and vegies, that cost has increased by
5 percent in just the last 12 months. Again, where is the priority of this Government? The
restrictions that are being put in place for people on benefits  are cost-saving measures
dressed up as help and encouragement. With the sole parent restrictions, sole parents are,
in fact, the group that is getting positive results right now. They have the highest number
of exits off that benefit and the lowest number of entries. What the Government wants to
do is make the sole parent benefit like the job seeker benefit. But the job seekers group
has one of the worst results. Where is the logic in that? Carmel Sepuloni mentioned the
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3577
impact of parents having to go back to work when their child is 3 years o ld and not 5
years old. Let us take a step back for a second and forget about whether that is the right
or the wrong thing to do, and let us ask what the social impact is for that child. What is
the social cost for that child of the parent leaving the house when the child is 3 years old
instead of 5 years old? Once the Government answers that question, it will also see the
priority that it has when dealing with child poverty and with the needy and the vulnerable
in our society.
As I said, the increase in the benefit is part of the solution; it is not a plan and it is not
the answer. I am looking forward to discussing this bill robustly in the Social Services
Committee, but at this stage, New Zealand First cannot support this bill.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: What a privilege to be able to stand to
speak this evening to the Support for Children in Hardship Bill, which gives effect to the
hardship package that we announced this afternoon. Listening to the attack from the other
side—I will tell you, earlier today when Bill English was giving that Budget speech, you
could really see from the back of the House the impact that it was having, not only on this
side but particularly on the other side.
Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition referenced my name in a speech and said I was
“Mooller”—Todd “Mooller”. Well, it is actually Todd “Muller”. It rhymes with “muller”
as in “mullet”, and the people who looked like stunned mullets as we were outlining a
once-in-a-generational change were those on the other side of the House. It has been 43
years since benefits have risen, and it is this side of the House —it is this Government—
that has made—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Looked more like a dead fish.

items.speaker: TODD MULLER
items.text: Well, I am sure you will turn up with two dead fish next week, Mr
Parker. It will happen. But, seriously, we have seen quite an afternoon here, and what a
tremendous bill to be able to stand up and talk to this afternoon.
What a change that we can talk to. The first rise in 43 years —$25 a week for those
with families on benefits and, immediately, it gets ridiculed by the other side. It is
significant money and it talks of a Government that cares, and when the Government is
in a position to respond to the needs of New Zealand, it does. We were handed an absolute
cot-case of an economy. It has taken 6 years to get to this position, and now we are in that
position to respond to the needs of New Zealanders. That is exactly what we have done,
and that is the reaction we are getting. The Opposition members know it, from the reaction
that is going on outside.
This is a very, very good bill. It is great to be able to talk to it —194,000 jobs since
2011. The reason I say that is important is it means there are 42,000 fewer children living
in welfare-dependent homes. We are making a difference and, therefore, we ca n put a
package like this in place to encourage those who are still yet to make that journey to be
able to do it. We will stand beside them and make sure that in their hour of need we are
there. We are running an economy that enables them to move from welfare to work. This
Government is working, we have a plan that is working, and I cannot wait to support this
bill through the various stages of the select committee. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: It is always interesting to reflect on wealthy
people’s understanding of poverty. There is a tone that I think possibly comes from greed
dependency. We hear a lot about benefit dependency but we do not acknowledge greed
dependency in our country, and it is quite a problem. We will be supporting this bill in its
first reading to the select committee because of the 25 bucks, because we cannot deprive
people of that , but there is still a misunderstanding of the issue when the scale of the
problem is so much greater than the supposed plan and the supposed solution. I would
rather not talk about mullets or anything else today; I would like to talk about the kids.
Today is in some ways a victory for the amazing group effort out there in the community
3578 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
to make child poverty such an important issue that the Government was unable to deny
it. I would like to pay tribute to people like the Child Poverty Action Group, Every Child
Counts, the New Zealand Council of Social Services, Unicef, and many more, and t he
Green Party, for our leadership through Metiria Turei’s unfailing and absolutely
determined commitment to make child poverty an issue that this Government could not
afford to ignore in this Budget because the focus groups told it that it could not afford it.
So before we get all warm -hearted about the caring Government, let us just
acknowledge that this campaign has achieved a small step. The step that has been
achieved, which is really important tonight, is an acknowledgment that income matters. I
have sat in this House for the last 6½ years hearing how poverty has got nothing to do
with money; it is all about individuals not pulling up their own bootstraps, it is all about
the failure of the education system and teachers, and it is all about people not grabbi ng
opportunity. Anybody who has worked at the front line of inequality in this country knows
that income is critical. The Government has been forced to give 25 bucks more a week
after 43 years. I am not the world’s greatest mathematician but anyone can tell that that
is not going to be enough after 43 years of Governments failing to lift the benefit. But we
are not going to look this tiny little gift -pony in the mouth because, actually, any money
in the hands of families right now is good. They need it but it is not a solution. So we
would like to just acknowledge that it is not a solution; it is a tiny little step. The solutions
have to be much more structural and much more generous.
If we can afford the nauseating tax cuts of several Budgets ago for the wealthiest
people, we could actually afford to extend the in-work tax credit to the families who really
need it. That would be a generous move. That would be a structural move. Instead of that
we have got giving on one hand and taking from the other. On the one hand there is this
extra money; on the other hand there is an increased obligation. An increased obligation
is always a euphemism for going down to Work and Income for another ri tual of
humiliation. Those of us who have worked as beneficiary advocates are under no illusions
about that experience. It is worse for the people who actually have to do it, but we have
witnessed it, and what we have seen is desperate families, including many solo parents,
particularly women -led families, being told they are failures and that they will be
sanctioned if they do not get work. In this bill they now have to have 20 hours’ work a
week. No amount of description of the obligation as “Oh, we’ll be  flexible about this.”
cuts any ice. We can sit in this House and use that language but go down to Work and
Income and witness what actually happens when families with no money are forced into
social obligation.
Let me talk about early childhood  education. The Green Party has demonstrated, just
by reading the officials’ briefing documents, that participation in early childhood
education is not sufficient; it is quality. But now we are going to make parents with a 3 -
year-old look for more work while the children must be in early childhood education of
whatever quality. Until we commit to the family-centred models that my colleague talked
about, like kōhanga, playcentre, and kindergarten, which are losing families all the time,
we are going to be putting kids into some good services and some utterly indifferent ones.
If we do not listen to the Brainwave Trust about what is important to the child in its first
few years, if we will not listen to the child experts, if we will not listen to the Children’s
Commissioner, if we will not listen to Jonathan Boston, who said today, reading the bill,
that actually a number of t he measures of poverty are failed under this bill and that the
$25 will not make a difference —if we will not listen to those people because we are so
inside our privileged little bubble of “We’ve done a nice thing today.” then we are failing
the kids of this country. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: I rise to support the Support for Children in Hardship
Bill because something is better than nothing. Still, I think, in this context, we can see
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3579
once again just how little value this National Government puts on parenting. I think that
this bill, more than any other bill, really demonstrates this. Work, in the Government’s
view, is not the very important and valuable work of raising children. That i s seen as
being not nearly as valuable as, maybe, a zero-hour contract for 20 hours a week. Let us
be honest: for anyone who really knows, or who is in touch with, what is going on out in
the community, these types of provisions, where people who are in re ceipt of a benefit
are forced out to work—and this bill forces them to go out and seek part -time jobs from
the time that their child is 3 years old —are driving a sort of employment market that,
actually, most New Zealanders are embarrassed and ashamed about. It is forcing the type
of labour market that sees the growth of zero -hour contracts and that sees the growth of
our low-wage economy.
I come from Hamilton, and the sort of growth in jobs that we are seeing in Hamilton
is that a new Wendy’s or a new Carl’s Jr has gone up —at the same time, scientists are
being made redundant from Ruakura Research Centre. So we are getting rid of our high-
value jobs and we are getting these minimum wage, zero -hour contract - type jobs. And
these are exactly the sorts of jobs that the Government is now forcing parents into when
many of these parents have made the decision that they would rather spend the time—or
that they need to spend their time —with their young children. This bill does not make
any differentiation for parents in receipt of a benefit who are raising children with
disabilities or with special needs. They, too, when their child is the age of 3 years, need
to go out and pound the streets and look for zero -hour contract work, up to —now—20
hours. I am not sure why the Government, when it required 15 hours of part -time work
before, now suddenly thinks that this can just leap to 20 hours’ work withou t it doing
anything to grow jobs in our economy—because that is the other area where this Budget
fails miserably.
It is of some merit that the Government has increased benefits for families with
children by $25 a week, but—and here is the but—it is a bit of a swings and roundabouts
thing, because it is requiring these same parents to go out and seek these part -time jobs
when their child turns 3 years old. They are going to have to pay more than $25 a week
in childcare fees to enable them to do that. So there is the $25 —and some —gone
straightaway. So I think that although it is always good to see families with children get
some more support from the Budget, in this instance, I think that we will find that this
money disappears very quickly. It will evaporate with the other mean approaches that this
Government is taking to cut spending in various areas.
I am speaking on this bill because I am Labour’s spokesperson on women’s affairs,
and this Budget will have quite a severe impact on women and their role in parenting. I
just want to make sure that the House notes that although the $25 a week in this bill is
good—and we certainly support that —we have some real concerns about some of the
other measures. At the same time, the Ministry for Women has taken a budget cut in this
Budget. It has a tiny little budget to start off with, and there it is: women, again, not being
taken seriously by this Government and having their hopes, dreams, and aspirations
dashed by a miserable approach from this Government. Labour supports this bill but we
think it does not go nearly far enough.

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: For the last 12 months, since I announced that I was
going to run for the National Party, I have been approached by a lot of people asking:
“Why would you be doing that? Why would someone with a degree in social work be
joining the National Party? Why wou ld you get involved?”. After today’s Budget, I do
not think I will be getting those questions any more. Today, in this Budget, this
Government has raised—has raised—for the first time in 43 years, the real bottom -line
benefits for people with families.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: How many years?
3580 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015

items.speaker: JONO NAYLOR
items.text: 43 years. The question we have to ask is: why now? I have heard
that asked from across the other side of the House today: “Why now?”. Well, I can tell
you why now. It is because we have been able to grow the economy over recent times.
We have been able t o grow the minimum wage —we have been able to grow the gap
between wages and what people are earning on benefits—to such a level that we can now
raise benefits without disincentivising people to go to work. That is what happens when
you have got a Minister of Finance who understands families and who understands how
an economy works: you can have a Government that is working hard to ensure that all of
these pieces of the jigsaw fit together to make a country that works hard and that i s
delivering the kinds of outcomes that New Zealanders want.
We find ourselves now in a position where families who are struggling, those who are
on low incomes —and we all know that there are families who are struggling in our
communities—will get more money in their pockets through an increase in Working for
Families. And those who are unable to work at the moment will see a greater amount of
money go into their bank accounts each week to enable them to start to lift themselves
out of the place that they find themselves in. That is why I am supporting this bill, that is
why I am glad to hear others in this House are supporting this bill, and I look forward to
discussing it with the select committee and to bringing it back to this House so that we
can continue to make good progress for families in New Zealand. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: This is the Government’s
seventh Budget. It promised a surplus some 6 years ago, and we have not seen it. More
important, we are sitting here, after the Budget has been read, debating benefits not jobs.
We would be debating jobs if National were doing its  job, and it is not. What we know
is: given that the Government said the rock star economy would benefit far more New
Zealanders in th e regions, we should be debating jobs here today, but we are debating
benefits. I wish we were debating the “Child Opportunity Bill”, and that the recognition
of poverty in this country meant that we would be talking about more than just $25. We
would be t alking about warm homes. We would be talking about jobs in our regions,
communities, and small towns. We would be talking about how to support those children
who are the most vulnerable learners, instead of supporting charter schools. We would be
talking a bout how we could support children and parents who have multiple
vulnerabilities and want a hand up, not a handout. This is an “ Oliver Twist Budget” and
we are debating $25 more going to vulnerable children. Well, we will take it. We will
take it, but do not expect anybody on this side of the House to say “Thank you very
much.”

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: Ah!

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: Why? Because it does not fix the multiple issues facing
vulnerable families and poor families out there in the community. Chris Bishop sighs.
Chris Bishop sighs because he would prefer this side of the House to say thank you. In
fact, the Children’s Commissioner puts it far better than I could. Dr Russell Wills himself
said: “I wasn’t expecting Government to increase incomes for … children. … Let’s be
clear, a one -off increase is not a plan for child poverty. … What we need is a
comprehensive plan to reduce child poverty.” That comes from the Children’s
Commissioner. He himself recognises that an isolated payment of $25 cannot fix all the
issues. But we will take it, and we will take it because we know the hardships that  are
faced by many children and families in the community, in small towns, and we know that
they need it.
But will it make a difference? I suspect not if we require parents to be work tested
when their youngest child is 3 years old. Let me share a story. We are talking about a
mother who goes to kōhanga and who volunteers her time because she is worried about
the type of life her child will have and she knows that getting an education will make a
21 May 2015 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 3581
difference. She has to be work tested when her child turns 3. She could make a critical
difference to supporting the education pathway of her under-5-year-old child if she were
able to continue to be the mother that she wants to be. The bill makes a number  of other
changes. We will get it to the select committee so that we can identify these types of
issues, which will, I think, start to unstitch some of the challenges of how to implement
it.
The other thing about the bill is that it really does not address some of the aspects that
are really fundamental to work. In these days and times for people who are required to be
work tested—when there are no new jobs in towns and communities, and when p eople
have to make changes to go to where there is work and they have to pay for childcare
because they have got no support network of family to be able to help them raise their
children—$25 will not make much of a difference. That is the reality—that is the reality.
In fact, I heard a constituent say “I want to be work tested because I want a job, but, God,
it’s demoralising. I go in there for my regular appointments and I have to answer the same
questions and go through the same types of box -ticking tests.” She said to me: “It’s just
demoralising. Give me anything. Give me a meaningful job, because I want to be able to
support my children and give them more.” But the jobs are just not there.
Sue and I are both from the Waikato. We understand the realities of what is not
happening in the region.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Sue Moroney.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: Sue Moroney. Sorry to my fellow colleague. We are both
from the Waikato. We understand the realities. In our area, there have been more job cuts
than jobs created, and the types of jobs that people are having to consider are the jobs that
do not really g ive them certainty. This is the challenge. With the 90 -day bill, being
employed for 3 months is not a full -time job; it is just living from hand to mouth —hand
to mouth.
This bill should go to a select committee. I am pleased that it is going there, because
there are aspects of the bill that need to be looked at further to ensure that what is intended
will actually make a critical difference to the lives of people. Just yesterday I was one of
several MPs who were out on the steps of Parliament receiving a petition from
ActionStation. I want to thank ActionStation for its efforts. It is a collective of
organisations committed to putting child poverty on the agenda. It identified that far more
needs to be done and that the Government needs a plan. This is an area in which those
260,000 children living in poverty will increase unless we do something meaningful and
comprehensive over a long period of time. We do not want to see that happen in a country
like New Zealand.
It is very important that people understand the parts of this bill that the Government is
trying to implement. The other aspect is being work -ready and work tested for part-time
work. I think about this provision in relation to childcare provisions and the practicalities
that exist in small communities. It will be very difficult if a person has childcare
provisions in the place where they live—say 26 kilometres out of their main city centre—
and has to travel 26 kilometres for their part -time work. It will be very difficult to make
those provisions fit with childcare and their preschool arrangements. I know. I live in a
small town. I have tried to find those types of arrangements. But, more important, for
people who do not have a natural family support network where they live, this is going to
be an impractical type of measure, about which I think we will see many people express
some concern. At the end of the day, I think if we want to support families and children,
especially those who are the most vulnerable, the changes need to be able to fit them, as
well as ensure that they are given a hand up and not a handout.
There are simply not enough afterschool childcare opportunities. For example, when
an early childhood centre or a kōhanga finishes at 3 o’clock, in some small towns you
3582 Support for Children in Hardship Bill 21 May 2015
will not get early childhood centres that can take them from 3 p.m. to 5.30 p.m. In some
communities, that it is just not the reality. And where there is the opportunity to have that,
you have to pay a lot of money—more than $25. Those are some of the practical aspects
of what the Government is intending to do—that is, work test people to go into part-time
work—and the reality of having children who need preschool education and then
afterschool care. These are some really important things that the Government needs to be
mindful of.
We are not going to knock the bill to the extent that $25 will not make a difference,
but the issue for me is whether it will make a critical difference. I suspect not. It is a
change. It is an increase. There is no doubt about that. But when you look at the real costs
of childcare, the real costs to someone who has no car of their own and is using public
transport to get to a job, $25 will not cover much more than an extra bit of bread and some
milk, hopefully—and they are still going to have to think about other pressures.
The challenge as well, when we talk about vulnerable families —families with more
than one child—is that you are doubling up on the cost of shoes, especially in winter, of
warm clothes, and of kai. If we are really true to what we are hearing in the communi ty,
there are already significant cost of living pressures on families who are paying a heck of
a lot—a heck of a lot —in private rentals. Twenty -five dollars is something, but will it
make a vital difference? I suspect not. I do not want to look a gift-horse in the mouth and
say “Pooh, pooh!” all the way through. It is pleasing to see that some effort has gone into
recognising that child poverty exists; the extent of which, I challenge the Government,
should not be minimised by the piecemeal approach that i t is taking here today. I look
forward to hearing the deliberations of the select committee and to identifying how, in
fact, in terms of the implementation of the bill, it will make a difference to the lives of
needy children. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Dr PARMJEET PARMAR
items.text: I feel so proud to be a part of this
Government, led by the Rt Hon John Key. I would like to congratulate our Deputy Prime
Minister and Minister of Finance, the Hon Bill English, on keeping New Zealand on track
for such solid economic growth.
It is a pleasure to take this call to support the Support for Children in Hardship Bill in
its first reading. This National Government has been, and is always, focused on delivering
for families and children, because we understand their needs. We also understand the
importance of a strong economy, because we know that it is this strong econo my, under
this National Government, that is allowing us to commit this package to help children in
hardship. New Zealand families also understand the importance of a strong economy.
This Budget allocates $790 million in this package, which is aimed to help children in
hardship—some of those children who are in New Zealand’s poorest families. Yes, there
is this additional support being provided to these children raised in these households, but
at the same time we want to support families to get out from welfare dependency. We
want to break that cycle of welfare dependency because we know that work is the pathway
to success in life. That is why we want to get more and more people into work as soon as
possible. Moving to paid work is the best way to lift more families out of poverty.
Although an increase in benefit rates will help address the concern about children
whose family’s resources have been falling behind those of other households, over many
years, if we compare families dependent on benefits versus families getting into work,  it
is clear that the financial circumstances of families dependent on benefits do not change
much over time, whereas the circumstances of families who get into work do change over
time. We know that in the past year 74,000 more people are in work and the average wage
has gone up by 2.1 percent, whereas inflation is negligible at 0.1 percent. National is
focused on sustainable growth, which is needed to support more jobs and higher incomes.
I support the bill and commend it to the House. Thank you.
